title: Clean Code Framework - Aggregated Coding Standards
description: Single source of truth aggregated and de-duplicated from 9 canonical software engineering books. Operating language is English. Principles are actionable directives for the coding agent, grouped by theme. Each rule lists the books that support it.

severityLevels.must: Hard rule. Do not violate without explicit user approval.
severityLevels.should: Strong default. Deviate only with a stated reason.
severityLevels.consider: Heuristic worth weighing for the given context.

principles.rule: Use intention-revealing, pronounceable, searchable names from the problem/domain vocabulary. Classes are nouns, methods are verbs. Rename when a name no longer fits.
Express intent in code, not comments. Delete commented-out/dead code. Keep only legal, intent, warning, TODO, and API-doc comments.
Keep functions small and do exactly one thing at a single level of abstraction. Minimize arguments (0-2 ideal); no boolean flag arguments.
No side effects in queries; apply Command-Query Separation and prefer side-effect-free functions.
Follow the rules of simple design in order: passes all tests, no duplication, expresses intent, minimal classes/methods. Avoid speculative generality and overengineering.
Simplify conditionals with guard clauses; replace type-switch conditionals with polymorphism where it clarifies behavior.
DRY: every piece of knowledge has a single authoritative representation. Remove duplication by the third occurrence (Rule of Three).
Depend on abstractions, not concretions. Program to interfaces; inject dependencies; avoid global mutable state and singletons in core logic.
Follow the Dependency Rule: source dependencies point inward toward higher-level policy. Business logic must not import frameworks, DB, web, or UI.
Keep components orthogonal and loosely coupled: keep strong connascence local, weaken coupling across boundaries. Apply Tell-Don't-Ask and the Law of Demeter; no train-wreck chains.
No cyclic dependencies between components; the component dependency graph must be a DAG. Depend in the direction of stability and abstraction.
Favor composition over inheritance; use inheritance only for true is-a relationships honoring Liskov substitutability.
Interface Segregation: depend only on what you use; prefer narrow, client-specific interfaces.
Single Responsibility: each module/class is responsible to one actor and has one reason to change. Keep classes small and cohesive.
Open-Closed: add behavior by adding code (extension points/polymorphism), not by modifying working code. Encapsulate what varies.
Draw boundaries between things that change for different reasons/rates; cross them only through well-defined interfaces. Wrap third-party APIs behind your own adapters.
Partition into well-bounded components with clear responsibilities; prefer domain-based partitioning. Make structure scream the domain, not the framework.

Use the Ubiquitous Language in code. Distinguish Entities (identity) from Value Objects (immutable, attribute-defined). Model aggregates with a single root as the consistency boundary; keep persistence behind repositories/factories.
Representation is the essence of programming: design the right data structures first; data design simplifies algorithms.
Prefer exceptions to error codes; do not return or pass null (use special-case objects). Provide context with errors and isolate error handling.
Crash early with Design by Contract: make pre/postconditions and invariants explicit via assertions; fail fast instead of continuing in a corrupt state. Never swallow errors silently.

Keep tests clean and first-class. Tests are FIRST (Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely), one concept each. A test is the first user of your code; prefer test-driven design and automate tests.
Maintain self-testing code as the safety net for refactoring; reproduce every bug with a test before fixing it.
Design for testability: use the Humble Object pattern to separate hard-to-test code (views, I/O) from testable logic.
Refactor in small behavior-preserving steps with green tests after each step. Wear one hat at a time: never mix feature changes and refactoring in one commit.
Refactor early and often. Use preparatory refactoring to make a hard change easy. Read code smells as signals and don't live with broken windows.
Good design is Easier To Change (ETC). Keep options open and decisions reversible; maximize decisions NOT yet made and minimize effort to build and maintain.
Apply the Boy Scout Rule: leave the code cleaner than you found it.
Conceptual integrity first: every solution follows one clear, coherent design concept. Consistency beats feature count and cleverness.
Work iteratively, not waterfall. Build a thin working end-to-end version first (tracer bullets), then refine. Treat first cuts/prototypes as disposable learning.
Be empirical and explicit: validate risky assumptions with prototypes/tests, and make assumptions explicit ('better wrong than vague'). Don't program by coincidence; only ship code you understand.
Everything is a trade-off: present significant decisions with explicit pros/cons and record the rationale (why matters more than how). Choose by context, not fashion.
Use constraints as friends: budget the critical scarce resource explicitly and let limits focus the design. Prioritize a small set of driving quality attributes; resist scope creep.
Invest the most care in the few bold, high-leverage decisions; they determine most of the outcome's quality. Design the bugs out through clear structure.
No silver bullet: manage essential complexity through thoughtful design, not tool worship.
